claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by suppressed atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy and nanoscale grain boundaries or interfaces synergistically suppress atomic diffusion.
The combination of high configurational entropy and nanoscale interfaces creates high activation-energy barriers against phase segregation.
High configurational entropy creates a flattened energy landscape.
The entropy-induced flattened energy landscape hampers atomic rearrangement.
Abundant nanoscale grain boundaries further restrict atomic diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion delays phase segregation and chemical decomposition at high temperature.
Near-equiatomic, well-mixed high-entropy nanoalloys are the relevant initial state for the proposed stability mechanism.
Thermally activated diffusion becomes significant at temperatures approaching approximately 0.8 times the melting temperature.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have lower diffusion rates than conventional low-entropy alloys under the same annealing conditions.
Fine-grained high-entropy nanoalloys will have lower diffusion rates than compositionally identical high-entropy alloys with larger grains.
High-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less grain growth than the proposed conventional-alloy or large-grain baselines.
High-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit delayed or reduced phase segregation relative to the proposed baselines.
The prediction applies below melting and not under conditions causing extensive degradation.
The prediction is limited to near-equiatomic nanoalloys, while substantial composition or processing deviations may produce different behavior.
Residual stresses and minor impurities may influence high-temperature stability.
The extent of grain growth can be used to quantify atomic diffusion rates in the proposed experiment.
Observing similar or faster diffusion, grain growth, and phase segregation in the nanoalloy relative to the controls would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes high activation-energy barriers, while the mechanism invokes a flattened energy landscape; the relationship between flattening the landscape and raising migration barriers is not explained and is conceptually in tension.
